CAS-001.q: Case – Electronics component plant: at year-end a model's finished goods (cost VND 6 billion) lost its main customer; management wants to keep the value since it 'could sell to others'. The auditor should prioritise:
CAS-001.e: Valuation is the key assertion; representations must be corroborated by independent evidence.
o: Requesting evidence of estimated selling prices (actual orders, post-year-end quotes), assessing NRV and proposing a write-down if needed
CAS-001.x:
Basis: VAS 02 paras 04, 19–20 (net realisable value); VSA 540; VSA 580 para 4.
Analysis: Loss of the main customer signals impairment → valuation is the key assertion. The 'can sell to others' claim must be backed by independent evidence: actual orders, quotes, post-year-end sales (VSA 560). If NRV < cost → propose a write-down (CAS-002).
Distractors: B – representations don't replace evidence (VSA 580); C – a count proves quantity, not value; D – writing off everything without basis is also wrong.

CAS-002.q: Case – An electronics component plant holds finished goods costing VND 6 billion after its main customer stopped ordering. After year-end an order covers 40% of the lot at 70% of cost; the rest is expected to fetch only 10% of cost as scrap; selling costs negligible. What inventory write-down is required (VND billion)?
CAS-002.x:
Basis: VAS 02 paras 04, 19 (NRV = estimated selling price − costs to complete − selling costs).
Working: NRV = ordered portion 6 × 40% × 70% + scrap portion 6 × 60% × 10% = 1.68 + 0.36 = 2.04 billion; write-down = 6 − 2.04 = VND 3.96 billion.
Analysis: The post-year-end order evidences conditions at 31 Dec (an adjusting event – VAS 23). Value each part of the batch separately because their selling prices differ.
Check: 2.04 + 3.96 = 6 ✓.

CAS-003.q: Case – A plastics plant uses standard costing. Large adverse material price variances sit in a suspense account at year-end. Select ALL risks/actions:
CAS-003.e: Inventory must reflect cost; standards may be used only if they approximate actual cost.
o: Allocate variances to inventory and COGS pro rata to reflect actual cost
Check whether variances were parked to reduce COGS and inflate profit
Assess the monthly variance review control
Leave them in suspense into next year
CAS-003.x:
Basis: VAS 02 para 07; IAS 2 para 21 (standard cost method).
Analysis: Standard costs may be used only if results approximate actual cost. A large unfavourable material price variance parked at year-end → (A) allocate it to inventory and COGS proportionally; (B) assess whether standards are outdated (prices have risen); (C) test whether parking aims to cut COGS and inflate profit; (D) evaluate the monthly variance review control.
Distractors: (E) Carrying it into next year misstates this year's COGS and inventory.

CAS-004.q: Case – A steel mill ran at only 55% of normal capacity due to weak orders. How are fixed production overheads of VND 120 billion treated?
CAS-004.e: Idle-capacity costs must not be pushed into inventory, inflating inventory and profit.
o: Absorbed into cost at normal capacity; the unabsorbed portion (idle capacity) is expensed in COGS
CAS-004.x:
Basis: VAS 02 para 08; IAS 2 para 13.
Analysis: Fixed production overheads are allocated on normal capacity. When output falls below normal, each unit absorbs only the normal-capacity rate; the unallocated part (idle capacity) is expensed in COGS for the period (CAS-005).
Distractors: B and D – allocating everything over low actual output inflates unit cost, pushing idle cost into inventory and inflating inventory and profit; C – it isn't an asset.

CAS-005.q: Case – A steel mill with normal capacity of 1 million tonnes/year produced only 550,000 tonnes this year due to weak orders; fixed production overheads are VND 120 billion. How much fixed overhead is expensed directly in COGS (not absorbed into inventory) (VND billion)?
CAS-005.e: Rate = 120 billion/1 million t = VND 120,000/t; absorbed 550,000 × 120,000 = 66 billion; expensed 120 − 66 = 54 billion VND.
CAS-005.x:
Basis: VAS 02 para 08.
Working: Rate = 120 billion / 1,000,000 tonnes = VND 120,000/tonne; absorbed = 550,000 × 120,000 = 66 billion; expensed directly = 120 − 66 = VND 54 billion.
Check: 54 / 120 = 45% = idle capacity (1 − 55%) ✓.
Analysis: The wrong method (120 billion over 550,000 tonnes) raises unit cost to ≈ VND 218,182/tonne and leaves idle cost in unsold inventory → inflated profit.

CAS-006.q: Case – An export garment maker does processing for a foreign principal that supplies the materials. A common FS error is:
CAS-006.e: Consigned materials are not controlled by the entity; track them off-balance sheet/disclose.
o: Recording the principal's materials as own inventory and revenue at finished-goods value instead of just the processing fee
CAS-006.x:
Basis: VAS 14; IFRS 15 paras B34–B38 (principal vs agent), B77; Circular 200/2014/TT-BTC (off-balance-sheet tracking of materials received for processing).
Analysis: Materials supplied by the principal aren't controlled by the garment maker → not its inventory; revenue is only the processing fee. A common error: recording received materials as inventory and revenue at finished-goods value → inflating assets, revenue and COGS. Received materials are tracked off-balance-sheet/disclosed.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the characteristic error.

CAS-007.q: Case – Internal audit at a chemicals plant finds: (1) the inbound weighbridge is operated by supplier staff; (2) no CCTV at the weighbridge; (3) handwritten weigh tickets. Select ALL risks and suitable controls:
CAS-007.e: The weighbridge is a key control point for bulk materials.
o: Risk of short receipts paid in full (collusion)
Electronic weighbridge linked to ERP, auto-printed non-editable tickets
CCTV and surprise weighbridge checks by QA/internal control
Reconcile weighed quantities to stock receipts and usage standards
Leave as is since the supplier is reputable
CAS-007.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10–11; ACFE.
Analysis: The weighbridge is the key control point for bulk materials. Three gaps (supplier staff weighing, no CCTV, handwritten slips) → (A) risk of short receipt but full payment, possibly collusive. Controls: (B) electronic scales linked to the ERP with auto-printed, uneditable slips; (C) CCTV and surprise scale checks by QA/IC (calibration); (D) reconcile weighed quantities with stock receipts and consumption standards.
Distractors: (E) Supplier reputation doesn't replace controls.

CAS-008.q: Case – A manufacturer replaces a costly mould (VND 2 billion, used for 400,000 units over 3 years). A sensible treatment:
CAS-008.e: Units-of-production reflects consumption of economic benefits well.
o: Recognise as PP&E (or prepayment if criteria aren't met) and allocate by units or useful life
Expense all in the month bought
CAS-008.x:
Basis: VAS 03 paras 06, 29–32; IAS 16 para 62; Circular 45/2013/TT-BTC (fixed-asset criteria – cost from VND 30 million, life over 1 year).
Analysis: A VND 2 billion mould used for 3 years → qualifies as a fixed asset (otherwise a prepaid expense amortised). Units-of-production depreciation (400,000 units) best reflects consumption because the mould wears with use (CAS-009).
Distractors: B – expensing at once misallocates cost across periods; C – a mould isn't a consumable material; D is wrong.

CAS-009.q: Case – A firm buys a production mould for VND 2 billion, expected to make 400,000 units over 3 years, depreciated by units of production. Year 1 output with the mould is 160,000 units. What is year-1 depreciation (VND million)?
CAS-009.x:
Basis: VAS 03 para 32 (units-of-production method); Circular 45/2013/TT-BTC.
Working: Year-1 depreciation = 2,000 × 160,000 / 400,000 = 2,000 × 40% = VND 800 million.
Analysis: Unit rate = 2,000 million / 400,000 = VND 5,000/unit × 160,000 = 800 million. Straight-line over 3 years would give 666.7 million – ignoring that year 1 used 40% of the mould's capacity.
Check: 800 / 2,000 = 40% = 160,000 / 400,000 ✓.

CAS-010.q: Case – A packaged food maker receives complaints about a contaminated December batch and recalls products in January. Effect on this year's FS:
CAS-010.e: The condition (defective product) existed at the reporting date.
o: Adjusting event (defect existed at production this year): provide for recall costs, reduce revenue/returns, write down remaining same-batch stock
CAS-010.x:
Basis: VAS 23 paras 08–09; VAS 18; IAS 37; IAS 10.
Analysis: A contaminated batch made and sold in December → the condition (defective product) existed at period-end; the January recall provides more evidence → an adjusting event: provide for recall, destruction and compensation costs (if reliably estimable); reduce revenue/record returns; write down remaining stock from the batch.
Distractors: B – disclosure only is for non-adjusting events; C and D use the wrong period.

CAS-011.q: Case – A 3-shift plant finds night-shift material usage 12% higher than day shift for the same product. A sensible internal audit approach:
CAS-011.e: Variances may be technical (machines, temperature) or losses; evidence is needed first.
o: Examine issues by shift, scrap, gate security and night CCTV; interview leaders; surprise counts
CAS-011.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10, P13; ACFE (CAS-007, FRD-074).
Analysis: 12% higher night-shift consumption may be technical (machines, temperature, skill) or leakage (less supervision at night). Approach: test stock issues by shift, scrap, gate security logs and night CCTV; interview supervisors and engineers; surprise end-of-shift counts – gathering evidence before concluding.
Distractors: B concludes without evidence; C ignores a red flag; D – raising the standard legitimises leakage.

CAS-012.q: Case – A manufacturer receives insurance compensation for a fire-damaged machine. The compensation is recognised as income when receivable, separately from the asset write-off (no netting).
CAS-012.e: True under IAS 16: impairment/derecognition and compensation are separate economic events.
CAS-012.x:
Basis: IAS 16 paras 65–66; VAS 03 (no offsetting – VAS 21 para 18).
Analysis: True. The asset loss (derecognising the damaged machine's carrying amount) and the insurance compensation are separate economic events: derecognise on damage; recognise compensation in income when it becomes receivable (virtually certain), without offsetting. Buying a replacement is a separate transaction at new cost.

CAS-013.q: Case – A new production line is trial-run for 2 months; trial output sells for VND 300 million. Under amended IAS 16, the proceeds:
CAS-013.e: Amended IAS 16 (effective 2022) prohibits deducting test-run proceeds from cost.
o: Are recognised in profit or loss with the related costs, not deducted from cost
CAS-013.x:
Basis: IAS 16 paras 17(e), 20A (amendment 'Proceeds before Intended Use', effective 1 Jan 2022).
Analysis: Under amended IAS 16, proceeds from selling items produced during testing go to profit or loss (revenue) with their production cost (per IAS 2), not as a deduction from the line's cost. Costs of testing whether the asset works properly are still capitalised.
Note: Under current Vietnamese practice (Circular 200), trial-run proceeds are usually deducted from investment cost – unlike IFRS.

CAS-014.q: Case – Auditing a manufacturer with large WIP valued using foreman-estimated completion percentages. Select ALL suitable procedures:
o: Attend WIP counts and observe actual completion
Assess the method and assumptions for completion estimates
Compare WIP value/output with prior periods
Test cut-off of transfers from WIP to finished goods
Accept the foreman's figures as expert
CAS-014.x:
Basis: VSA 501; VSA 540; VAS 02.
Analysis: Large WIP valued on a supervisor's percentage-of-completion estimate → a material estimate. Procedures: (A) attend the WIP count and observe actual completion; (B) evaluate the method and assumptions; (C) compare WIP/output with prior periods for anomalies; (D) test cut-off of transfers from WIP to finished goods.
Distractors: (E) Operators may be biased; estimates must be independently tested (VSA 540).

CAS-015.q: Case – A cement maker must restore a quarry after extraction. This year the restoration estimate rises due to new rules. The correct IFRS treatment:
CAS-015.e: Changes in decommissioning estimates adjust the asset under IFRIC 1 (cost model).
o: Increase the provision and the related asset cost (IFRIC 1), depreciating the increase over the remaining life
Expense the full increase this year
CAS-015.x:
Basis: IAS 37; IFRIC 1 para 5 (changes in decommissioning liabilities – cost model); IAS 16 para 16(c).
Analysis: A quarry restoration obligation is a provision (IAS 37) whose initial cost is capitalised into the asset (IAS 16). When the estimate rises due to new rules: increase the provision and the related asset's cost, depreciating the increase over the remaining life (prospectively). A decrease beyond carrying amount goes to profit or loss.
Distractors: B – immediate expensing breaches IFRIC 1; C – a present obligation must be recognised; D – it isn't the revaluation model.

CAS-016.q: Case – A plant buys imports FOB; goods were loaded at the port of shipment on 28/12 but reach the warehouse on 10/01. At 31/12 the entity:
CAS-016.e: Under FOB, risk and control pass to the buyer when goods are loaded on board.
o: Recognises goods in transit and the payable
CAS-016.x:
Basis: VAS 02; Incoterms 2020 (FOB – risk passes when goods are on board at the port of shipment); Circular 200/2014/TT-BTC (goods in transit).
Analysis: FOB origin: risk and control pass to the buyer once goods are loaded on board (28 Dec) → at 31 Dec the goods belong to the entity: record goods in transit and a payable, even though they arrive on 10 Jan.
Distractors: B – not recording understates assets and liabilities (cut-off error); C and D misstate the nature.
Note: Incoterms 2020 defines risk transfer as goods 'placed on board' (the old 'ship's rail' concept is gone).

CAS-017.q: Case – A plant contracted to supply 10,000 units at VND 500 thousand each; expected cost is now 560 thousand/unit due to material price rises; 4,000 units delivered. What onerous contract provision is needed for the remainder (VND million)?
CAS-017.e: 6,000 × (560 − 500) thousand = 360 million VND (assuming no cheaper exit).
CAS-017.x:
Basis: IAS 37 paras 66–69 (onerous contracts), 2020 amendment (costs of fulfilling include incremental and allocated directly related costs); VAS 18.
Working: Remaining = 10,000 − 4,000 = 6,000 units; unit loss = 560 − 500 = VND 60,000; provision = 6,000 × 60,000 = VND 360 million.
Analysis: The provision is the lower of the net cost of fulfilling and the cost of exiting; assumed no cheaper exit. Before providing, recognise impairment of assets dedicated to the contract (if any).
Check: 6,000 × (500 − 560) = −360 million ✓.

CAS-018.q: Case – An FDI manufacturer buys all materials from its foreign parent and sells all output back to it, making losses for years while expanding. The main risk for auditors/tax authorities:
CAS-018.e: Transfer pricing documentation and comparability analysis must be reviewed.
o: Transfer pricing – related-party prices not at arm's length; CIT and going concern implications
CAS-018.x:
Basis: Decree 132/2020/ND-CP (related-party transactions – arm's-length principle); VSA 550; VSA 570.
Analysis: Buying all inputs from and selling all output to the parent, loss-making for years yet expanding → transfer pricing signs: high purchase and low sale prices shifting profit abroad and reducing Vietnamese CIT. The tax authority may impose arm's-length prices. The auditor checks transfer-pricing documentation, comparables and related-party disclosures; assesses tax exposure (back taxes, penalties) and going concern (dependence on the parent).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the main risk.

CAS-019.q: Case – A pharma plant runs a product recall. Select ALL suitable controls and accounting:
CAS-019.e: Selling suspect goods is illegal and unethical.
o: Batch traceability to define recall scope
Provide for reliably estimated recall, destruction and compensation costs
Quarantine same-batch stock and assess write-downs
Disclose legal risk and contingent liabilities if not estimable
Keep selling suspect batches to recover cost
CAS-019.x:
Basis: IAS 37; VAS 18; COSO 2013; Pharmacy Law 2016 (drug recalls).
Analysis: In a recall: (A) trace by batch to define scope; (B) provide for recall, destruction and compensation costs if reliably estimable; (C) quarantine stock from the batch and assess write-downs; (D) disclose legal risks and contingent liabilities if not yet estimable.
Distractors: (E) Continuing to sell suspect batches breaches pharmacy law and ethics, endangering patients and creating far greater liability.

CAS-020.q: Case – A manufacturer has major periodic overhauls (kiln relined every 5 years) under IFRS. The treatment:
CAS-020.e: IAS 16 doesn't allow accruing future overhauls as there's no present obligation.
o: Capitalise the overhaul as a separate component and depreciate to the next overhaul; derecognise the remaining old overhaul
Accrue overhaul costs yearly as a liability
Expense all in the overhaul year
CAS-020.x:
Basis: IAS 16 paras 13–14 (replaced parts, major inspections); IAS 37 paras 18–19 (no provisions for future operating costs).
Analysis: Under IFRS, a kiln overhaul every 5 years is capitalised as a separate component when incurred and depreciated to the next overhaul; the previous overhaul's remaining carrying amount is derecognised. No accrual in advance – there's no present obligation (the entity could sell or stop using the kiln).
Distractors: B – pre-accrual breaches IFRS; C – expensing at once misallocates benefits; D is wrong.
Note: Vietnamese practice (Circular 200) allows accruing periodic major repairs – unlike IFRS.

CAS-021.q: Case – An electronics retailer receives volume rebates from suppliers on annual purchase targets. The correct recognition:
CAS-021.e: Supplier rebates reduce purchase cost; they aren't revenue.
o: Reduce inventory cost (and COGS when sold), accruing when achievement is probable
CAS-021.x:
Basis: VAS 02 para 07 (trade discounts and rebates deducted from purchase cost); IAS 2 para 11.
Analysis: Volume rebates from suppliers are trade discounts → reduce purchase cost: the share for goods still on hand reduces inventory, the share for goods sold reduces COGS (CAS-022). Accrue during the year when achievement is probable, not waiting for December.
Distractors: B – it isn't revenue (no distinct service to the supplier); C is wrong; D – a single December entry misstates timing and allocation.
Note: If the amount pays for a distinct service (display, advertising) at fair value, treatment differs.

CAS-022.q: Case – An electronics retailer earns a 2% volume rebate on annual purchases of VND 500 billion; at year-end 30% of the related goods remain in stock. How much of the rebate must reduce inventory (rather than COGS) (VND billion)?
CAS-022.e: Rebate = 500 × 2% = 10 billion; on goods still held = 10 × 30% = 3 billion; 7 billion reduces COGS.
CAS-022.x:
Basis: VAS 02 para 07.
Working: Total rebate = 500 × 2% = 10 billion; share for goods on hand = 10 × 30% = 3 billion (reduce inventory); share for goods sold = 10 × 70% = 7 billion (reduce COGS).
Analysis: Booking all 10 billion against COGS overstates this year's profit by 3 billion and leaves inventory above actual cost.
Check: 3 + 7 = 10 ✓.

CAS-023.q: Case – A consumer-goods distributor pays 'display support' to supermarkets and 'trade discounts' to tier-1 dealers. Select ALL accounting/control issues:
CAS-023.e: IFRS 15 treats consideration payable to a customer as a price reduction unless for distinct goods/services.
o: Payments to customers usually reduce revenue unless for a distinct service at fair value
Contracts and proof of display (photos, minutes) are needed
Risk of fake display payments in collusion with sales staff
Always book as selling expense without analysis
CAS-023.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras 70–72 (consideration payable to a customer); ACFE.
Analysis: (A) Payments to customers (display support, discounts) reduce revenue unless they buy a distinct good/service at fair value (then expense); (B) contracts and proof of display (photos, minutes) are needed; (C) risk of fake display payments colluding with sales staff; (D) year-end discount cut-off.
Distractors: (E) Defaulting to selling expense is wrong – it affects net revenue and gross margin.
Note: Under VAS 14, trade discounts are revenue deductions – a similar result.

CAS-024.q: Case – A 300-store convenience chain counts only its 30 largest stores at year-end. The auditor should:
CAS-024.e: Cycle counts can replace a full year-end count if controls are effective.
o: Assess in-year cycle-count controls, attend counts at additional sampled stores, analyse shrinkage by store
CAS-024.x:
Basis: VSA 501 paras 4–8, A8 (cycle counts).
Analysis: A year-end count at only 30 of 300 stores → most inventory isn't counted at year-end. Cycle counts during the year can substitute if controls are effective (adequate coverage, differences adjusted, reliable perpetual records). The auditor evaluates the cycle-count controls, attends additional stores (including small, high-shrink ones), analyses shrinkage by store and tests roll-forward to year-end.
Distractors: B – small stores together may be material; C is usually impractical; D is insufficient.

CAS-025.q: Case – A supermarket's loyalty scheme gives 1 point per VND 100 thousand spent, each point redeemable for 1 thousand; 80% expected redemption. Monthly sales VND 2,000 million, 20,000 points issued. What revenue is allocated to points (relative standalone price, rounded) (VND million)?
CAS-025.e: Points' standalone price = 20,000 × 1 thousand × 80% = 16 million; allocation = 2,000 × 16/(2,000 + 16) ≈ 15.87 million VND.
CAS-025.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras 73–80, B39–B43 (material rights; relative stand-alone selling price allocation).
Working: Stand-alone price of points = 20,000 × VND 1,000 × 80% = 16 million; allocated = 2,000 × 16 / (2,000 + 16) = 32,000 / 2,016 ≈ VND 15.87 million.
Analysis: 15.87 million is a contract liability, recognised as revenue on redemption or expiry; goods revenue for the month = 2,000 − 15.87 ≈ 1,984.13 million.
Check: 15.87 + 1,984.13 = 2,000 ✓.

CAS-026.q: Case – An e-commerce marketplace lists third-party sellers, collects payments on their behalf and earns an 8% fee; sellers set prices and bear inventory risk. The marketplace's revenue:
CAS-026.e: The platform doesn't control the goods before transfer to customers.
CAS-026.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras B34–B38 (principal versus agent).
Analysis: The marketplace doesn't control goods before transfer: sellers set prices, bear inventory risk and are primarily responsible → the platform is an agent, recognising net revenue – the 8% commission. Cash collected for sellers is a liability.
Distractors: B – gross recognition inflates revenue (GMV isn't revenue); C has the wrong timing; D is wrong.

CAS-027.q: Case – A pharma distributor has 5,000 pharmacy customers, rapidly rising overdue balances, and salespeople collecting cash at pharmacies. Select ALL significant risks:
CAS-027.e: Domestic customers pay in VND, so FX risk is negligible.
o: Fictitious sales to 'ghost' customers to meet KPIs
Near-expiry stock pushed to pharmacies then returned
CAS-027.x:
Basis: VSA 240; VSA 315; ACFE.
Analysis: 5,000 pharmacy customers, rising overdue receivables, cash collected by sales staff → significant risks: (A) lapping and theft of collections (FRD-011); (B) inadequate bad-debt allowance; (C) fictitious sales to 'ghost' customers to hit KPIs (FRD-060); (D) pushing near-expiry stock to pharmacies that later return it (channel stuffing – FRD-034).
Distractors: (E) Domestic customers pay in VND → FX risk is negligible.

CAS-028.q: Case – A fashion chain allows 30-day returns. December revenue is VND 50 billion; historical return rate 6%. At 31/12 the correct accounting:
CAS-028.e: Variable consideration (return rights) must be estimated when revenue is recognised.
o: Recognise a refund liability for expected returns and a right-to-recover asset at cost
CAS-028.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 para 55, B20–B27 (sales with a right of return).
Analysis: Return rights are variable consideration estimated at recognition: recognise revenue only for goods not expected back; record a refund liability for expected returns (CAS-029); record an asset for the right to recover goods at cost less recovery costs, reducing COGS accordingly.
Distractors: B and C use the wrong period, inflating December revenue; D is insufficient.

CAS-029.q: Case – A fashion chain allows 30-day returns. December revenue is VND 50 billion and the historical return rate is 6%. What refund liability is recognised at 31/12 (VND billion)?
CAS-029.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 para B21.
Working: Refund liability = 50 × 6% = VND 3 billion.
Analysis: December revenue recognised = 50 − 3 = 47 billion. Also record a return asset = cost of the 3 billion of expected returns (less recovery costs and value loss). The 6% must rest on reliable history adjusted for trends and be reassessed each period.
Check: 47 + 3 = 50 ✓.

CAS-030.q: Case – A car importer sells through dealers; dealers may return unsold cars after 6 months and the importer sets retail prices. On delivery to dealers:
CAS-030.e: IFRS 15 consignment indicators must be evaluated.
o: Control may not have passed (consignment) – assess return rights, price control and inventory risk before recognising revenue
When the dealer pays a deposit
CAS-030.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras B77–B78 (consignment arrangements), 38 (indicators of transfer of control).
Analysis: Consignment indicators: the importer controls goods until the dealer sells to end customers; can require return or transfer to another dealer; the dealer has no unconditional obligation to pay (returns allowed after 6 months); the importer sets retail prices. → Control may not pass on delivery to the dealer → no revenue yet.
Distractors: B, C and D recognise too early.

CAS-031.q: Case – Internal audit at a supermarket chain finds 15% of refunds lack original receipts, mostly by 3 evening cashiers. Select ALL suitable actions:
CAS-031.e: Verify before concluding and protect personal rights.
o: Review CCTV and POS data of the 3 cashiers
Require shift-manager approval of every refund
Allow refunds only with receipts or system verification
Report to the Audit Committee if fraud is verified
Publicly name the 3 cashiers before verification
CAS-031.x:
Basis: ACFE (refund fraud); COSO 2013 P10.
Analysis: 15% of refunds lacking original receipts, concentrated in three evening cashiers → a red flag for fictitious refunds (creating fake refunds and pocketing cash). Actions: (A) review CCTV and POS data for the three; (B) shift-manager approval for every refund; (C) refunds only with original receipts or system verification; (D) report to the audit committee if fraud is confirmed.
Distractors: (E) Naming them before verification breaches personal rights and creates legal risk (FRD-066).

CAS-032.q: Case – A retailer leases 200 premises; many leases have variable rent as a % of store sales on top of fixed rent. Under IFRS 16:
CAS-032.e: Sales-based variable payments are excluded from the lease liability.
o: Only fixed payments (and those linked to an index/rate) enter the lease liability; sales-based rent is expensed as incurred
All expected rent including % of sales enters the liability
CAS-032.x:
Basis: IFRS 16 paras 27–28, 38(b).
Analysis: Lease liabilities include fixed (and in-substance fixed) payments and variable payments depending on an index or rate. Payments based on a percentage of store sales are excluded → expensed as incurred.
Distractors: B – including expected sales-based rent breaches the standard; C – the fixed part must be recognised; D is wrong.
Note: Current VAS 06 still classifies leases as operating or finance; operating lessees expense rent with no lease liability.

CAS-033.q: Case – A distributor's largest customer holds 35% of receivables, is 150 days late and is restructuring bank debt. The auditor needs to:
o: Assess collectability: customer financials, post-year-end receipts, collateral; propose a suitable allowance and consider concentration disclosure
Accept since it's a big customer
CAS-033.x:
Basis: VSA 505; VSA 540; Circular 48/2019/TT-BTC (bad-debt provisioning by overdue period).
Analysis: A customer holding 35% of receivables, 150 days late and restructuring bank debt → high valuation risk. Procedures: the customer's financial information and restructuring status; post-year-end receipts; collateral and guarantees; propose an adequate allowance; disclose credit concentration.
Distractors: B – confirmations only prove existence (AUD-047); C – big customers can still fail; D – writing off without grounds is wrong.
Note: Circular 48/2019 sets rates by overdue period (e.g., 6 months to under 1 year: 30%); 150 days is short of 6 months, but an allowance can reflect expected loss when the debtor is in difficulty.

CAS-034.q: Case – A trader runs 'buy 2 get 1 free': the free item isn't a separate selling expense; revenue is allocated across all 3 items under IFRS 15.
CAS-034.e: True. It's a bundled sale; the 'free' item is part of the performance obligations (VAT rules may treat it separately).
CAS-034.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras 73–80 (allocating the transaction price); Circular 219/2013/TT-BTC, Decree 81/2018/ND-CP (promotional goods – VAT).
Analysis: True. 'Buy 2 get 1' is a bundle of three items sold for the price of two → the 'free' item is part of the performance obligations; revenue is allocated across all three by relative stand-alone prices, and all three costs go to COGS – not a separate selling expense.
Note: For VAT, promotional goods registered under trade rules may have a zero taxable value – tax treatment may differ from accounting.

CAS-035.q: Case – A pharmacy chain franchises rapidly, charging initial fees of VND 500 million/store covering training and a 5-year brand licence (which the franchisor keeps developing). Initial fee recognition:
CAS-035.e: A licence is a right to access when the licensor keeps affecting the IP.
o: Analyse obligations: distinct pre-opening services when delivered; brand access over 5 years
CAS-035.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras 22–30 (performance obligations), B56–B62 (licences – right to access versus right to use).
Analysis: The 500 million initial fee covers: start-up services (training) – if distinct, recognised when complete; a 5-year brand licence that the franchisor keeps developing and affecting → a 'right to access' licence, recognised over 5 years. Allocate by relative stand-alone prices.
Distractors: B – recognising all at signing is premature; C isn't a criterion; D is wrong.

CAS-036.q: Case – A distributor implements a new ERP; for the first 3 months many orders are processed 'off-system' in Excel. Select ALL audit risks:
o: Revenue and inventory may be incomplete or double-counted when back-loaded
Automated controls don't operate on off-system transactions
Migrated opening balances may be wrong
Fraud risk rises due to missing audit trails
Risk falls since the ERP is modern
CAS-036.x:
Basis: VSA 315 (IT, system change – AUD-016); VSA 240.
Analysis: Orders processed 'outside the system' in Excel during the first 3 ERP months → (A) revenue and inventory may be incomplete or duplicated when back-loaded; (B) automated controls (credit limits, pricing, duplicate blocks) don't apply off-system; (C) migrated opening balances may be wrong; (D) missing audit trails raise fraud risk.
Distractors: (E) Transition periods always increase risk, however modern the system.

CAS-037.q: Case – An importer pays in USD; the rate spikes at year-end; it owes USD 2 million. FS impact:
o: Retranslate the payable at the closing rate, recognise FX loss in finance costs; disclose FX risk
Add the loss to inventory cost
CAS-037.x:
Basis: VAS 10 paras 12–15; IAS 21 paras 23, 28; IFRS 7 (market risk disclosure); Circular 200/2014/TT-BTC (remeasuring foreign-currency monetary items, finance costs).
Analysis: A USD supplier payable is a monetary item → remeasure at the closing rate; a rising rate → a larger liability → an FX loss in finance costs (CAS-038); disclose FX risk and sensitivity.
Distractors: B – not remeasuring understates payables; C – post-recognition FX differences don't go into inventory cost; D – not equity (except special cases such as pre-operating periods under older rules).

CAS-038.q: Case – An importer owes a supplier USD 2 million recorded at VND 24,900/USD; the year-end revaluation rate is 25,450. What is the FX revaluation loss (VND million)?
CAS-038.x:
Basis: VAS 10 paras 12, 15; Circular 200/2014/TT-BTC (payables remeasured at the bank's selling rate).
Working: FX loss = 2,000,000 × (25,450 − 24,900) = 2,000,000 × 550 = VND 1,100,000,000 = 1,100 million.
Analysis: Dr finance costs / Cr trade payables 1,100 million. Check current tax rules on whether this unrealised loss on remeasured payables needs a CIT adjustment.
Check: USD 2 million × 25,450 = 50,900 million; × 24,900 = 49,800 million; difference 1,100 ✓.

CAS-039.q: Case – A large distributor has 40 provincial warehouses; local stock clerks can adjust inventory in the system. Analysis shows write-downs clustered before counts. A reasonable conclusion:
CAS-039.e: Adjustment rights must be separate from custodians and require approval with minutes.
o: Signs of concealing losses before counts; remove adjustment rights, centralise approval and investigate adjustments
CAS-039.x:
Basis: ACFE (FRD-022); COSO 2013 P10.
Analysis: Provincial stock accountants adjusting inventory themselves, with write-downs clustered just before counts → a sign of concealing losses: reducing records to match stock already taken so the count shows no difference. Action: withdraw their adjustment rights; require minutes and independent central approval; investigate past adjustments (preparer, items, value, timing).
Distractors: B, C and D can't explain the pre-count timing pattern.

CAS-040.q: Case – A retailer sells vouchers via an e-payment partner; proceeds from unused vouchers at year-end are recognised as contract liabilities.
CAS-040.e: True. Revenue is recognised on redemption (or breakage under IFRS 15).
CAS-040.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 para 106 (contract liabilities), B44–B47 (customers' unexercised rights – breakage).
Analysis: True. Cash from unused vouchers is an obligation to supply goods/services later → deferred revenue/contract liability. Revenue is recognised on redemption; expected breakage is recognised in proportion to redemption patterns if reliably estimable, or when redemption becomes remote.

CAS-041.q: Case – An apartment developer collects instalments before handover. Management wants over-time revenue under IFRS 15. The condition is:
CAS-041.e: The enforceable right to payment must be assessed under each market's law and contracts.
o: The asset has no alternative use to the entity and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for work done (even if the customer cancels)
CAS-041.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras 35(c), 36–37, B9–B13.
Analysis: Over-time recognition under criterion 35(c) requires: (1) no alternative use to the entity (the specific sold unit, restricted by contract/law from redirection); and (2) an enforceable right to payment for performance to date, even if the customer terminates (other than for the entity's failure).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't IFRS 15 conditions.
Note: The payment right must be assessed under real-estate law and the specific contract (CAS-059).

CAS-042.q: Case – A contractor: contract price VND 800 billion; costs to date 300 billion; estimated costs to complete 300 billion. What cumulative revenue is recognised under the cost-to-cost (input) method (VND billion)?
CAS-042.x:
Basis: VAS 15 para 30; IFRS 15 paras B18–B19 (input method).
Working: Total expected cost = 300 + 300 = 600 billion; completion = 300 / 600 = 50%; cumulative revenue = 800 × 50% = VND 400 billion.
Analysis: Cumulative gross profit = 400 − 300 = 100 billion (25% margin = (800 − 600)/800). Reliability hinges on the cost-to-complete estimate – a material estimate (AUD-045).
Check: 100 / 400 = 25% ✓.

CAS-043.q: Case – A contractor: contract price VND 800 billion; costs to date 300 billion, of which 60 billion is uninstalled materials delivered to site (not made by the entity); total expected costs 600 billion. What is the cost-based progress after excluding uninstalled materials (%, 2 decimals)?
CAS-043.e: Excluding uninstalled materials: (300 − 60)/(600 − 60) = 240/540 ≈ 44.44% (revenue on uninstalled materials may be recognised at cost if criteria are met).
CAS-043.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 para B19(b) (uninstalled materials).
Working: Completion = (300 − 60) / (600 − 60) = 240 / 540 ≈ 44.44%.
Analysis: Uninstalled materials don't depict progress → exclude them from numerator and denominator. Revenue for them may be recognised at cost (zero margin) if the materials aren't distinct, the customer controls them before installation, their cost is significant, and the entity didn't design/manufacture them. Revenue = 44.44% × (800 − 60) + 60 ≈ 328.9 + 60 = 388.9 billion (if conditions are met).
Check: 540 × 44.44% ≈ 240 ✓.

CAS-044.q: Case – Auditing a contractor that booked revenue on many 'variation claims' not yet approved by the employer. Select ALL suitable procedures/assessments:
CAS-044.e: Unapproved variations are material estimates prone to abuse.
o: Assess contract modification criteria: enforceability, highly probable no significant reversal
Inspect claims, meeting minutes with the employer, approval precedents
Recognise all since work is done
CAS-044.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras 18–21 (contract modifications), 56–58 (constraining variable consideration); VSA 540; VSA 505.
Analysis: Unapproved variations already booked as revenue → a material, easily abused estimate. Procedures: (A) assess whether the modification is enforceable and a significant reversal is highly improbable; (B) examine proposals, meeting minutes and approval precedents; (C) confirm directly with the employer; (D) apply the variable consideration constraint.
Distractors: (E) Completing the work doesn't mean there's a right to payment.

CAS-045.q: Case – A developer holds an office tower for rental (investment property). Under current VAS, it is presented:
CAS-045.e: VAS 05 uses the cost model; IAS 40 allows a choice of cost or fair value.
o: At cost, depreciated; fair value disclosed if determinable
CAS-045.x:
Basis: VAS 05 paras 18–19, 30, 40 (investment property – cost model, fair value disclosure); IAS 40.
Analysis: Under VAS 05, investment property is carried at cost and depreciated (except property held for capital appreciation, which under Circular 200 isn't depreciated but tested for impairment), with fair value disclosed if determinable. IAS 40 allows a choice of cost or fair value.
Distractors: B – fair value without depreciation is an IAS 40 option, not VAS; C – it isn't inventory since it's held for rent; D is wrong.

CAS-046.q: Case – A developer holds large project WIP inventory; the market is slow and secondary prices fell 20%. The key audit procedure:
CAS-046.e: Legal delays or prolonged projects raise costs and lower NRV.
o: Assess each project's NRV: expected prices (recent deals, valuations), costs to complete, selling costs, legal progress
CAS-046.x:
Basis: VAS 02 paras 19–20; VSA 540.
Analysis: A sluggish market with secondary prices down 20% → risk that NRV < cost. Key procedure: NRV per project = expected selling price (recent deals, independent valuations) − costs to complete − selling costs; consider legal progress (prolonged legal hurdles raise holding costs and cut value) – CAS-047.
Distractors: B – accumulated cost is only cost; C is an unsupported assumption; D is insufficient.

CAS-047.q: Case – A developer has project WIP costing VND 1,200 billion; cost to complete 500 billion; expected revenue after price cuts 1,600 billion; selling costs 5% of revenue. What write-down is required (VND billion)?
CAS-047.x:
Basis: VAS 02 paras 04, 19.
Working: Selling costs = 1,600 × 5% = 80 billion; NRV = 1,600 − 500 − 80 = 1,020 billion; write-down = cost 1,200 − 1,020 = VND 180 billion.
Analysis: Costs to complete are deducted because the unfinished project can't be sold as is. Sensitivity: a further 5% price drop (80 billion) lifts the write-down to about 256 billion.
Check: 1,020 + 180 = 1,200 ✓.

CAS-048.q: Case – A developer collects 'reservation deposits' before the project is legally eligible for sale and immediately 'lends' them to the chairman's related company. Select ALL risks:
CAS-048.e: It combines compliance, fraud and liquidity risks.
o: Breach of real estate law on collecting money
Misuse of funds via related parties, risk of loss
Going concern risk if the project stalls and buyers demand refunds
No risk since it's customers' money
CAS-048.x:
Basis: Law on Real Estate Business 2023 (conditions for deposits and off-plan sales); VSA 250; VSA 550; VSA 570.
Analysis: Taking 'reservation deposits' before the project qualifies for sale and passing them to the chair's related company as a 'temporary loan' → (A) breaches real-estate rules on collecting money; (B) misappropriation via a related party with loss risk; (C) unapproved/undisclosed related-party transactions; (D) going-concern risk if the project stalls and buyers demand refunds.
Distractors: (E) Customer money is a repayment obligation – misusing it creates major risk.
Note: The 2023 Law (effective 1 Aug 2024) tightly limits deposits (max 5% of price, only once the project qualifies) – check the original text.

CAS-049.q: Case – A contractor receives a 20% advance from the employer. The advance is recognised as:
CAS-049.e: No revenue until the related obligation is performed.
o: A liability (customer advance/contract liability), offset as work is certified
CAS-049.x:
Basis: VAS 15; IFRS 15 para 106 (contract liabilities); Circular 200/2014/TT-BTC (customer advances).
Analysis: A 20% advance received before performing → a liability (customer advance/contract liability), offset progressively against certified payments. No performance means no revenue.
Distractors: B and C recognise revenue/income early; D – it isn't equity.
Note: Large, long-dated advances may contain a financing component under IFRS 15 paras 60–65.

CAS-050.q: Case – An employer retains 5% of payments as a 2-year warranty retention. Work certified this year is VND 400 billion. What retention receivable does the contractor have (VND billion)?
CAS-050.e: 400 × 5% = 20 billion VND; classified non-current if due after 12 months.
CAS-050.x:
Basis: VAS 15; VAS 21 (current/non-current classification); Decree 06/2021/ND-CP (construction warranties).
Working: Retention = 400 × 5% = VND 20 billion.
Analysis: The contractor records a 20 billion retention receivable (revenue of 400 billion already recognised on certification); classify it non-current if collected after 12 months (2-year warranty). Assess collectability (the employer may deduct repair costs) and the contractor's own warranty provision.
Check: 400 − 20 = 380 billion paid now ✓.

CAS-051.q: Case – A developer keeps capitalising interest although construction has been halted for 10 months due to permits. Assessment:
CAS-051.e: Improper capitalisation inflates assets and profit.
o: Capitalisation must be suspended during extended abnormal interruptions; expense the interest
CAS-051.x:
Basis: VAS 16 paras 18–20 (suspending capitalisation); IAS 23 paras 20–21.
Analysis: Borrowing-cost capitalisation must be suspended during extended abnormal interruptions (VAS 16 cites over 3 months), unless the pause is a necessary part of the process. A 10-month halt over permits → interest for that period goes to finance costs. Continuing to capitalise inflates the project and profit.
Distractors: B breaches the standard; C – disclosure doesn't fix the error; D is wrong.

CAS-052.q: Case – Internal audit at a builder reviews subcontractor quantity certification. Select ALL effective controls:
CAS-052.e: Self-certification with self-approval is an SoD conflict.
o: Match certified quantities to as-built drawings and site diaries
Unit prices per approved contract, variations separately approved
Site manager self-certifies and approves payment
CAS-052.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10; ACFE; Decree 06/2021/ND-CP (construction quality and acceptance).
Analysis: Subcontractor quantity certification controls: (A) confirmation by independent supervisors (consultant, QS); (B) matching certified quantities to as-built drawings and site diaries; (C) unit rates per approved contracts, with variations approved separately; (D) periodic photo/drone progress records – independent, time-stamped evidence.
Distractors: (E) A site manager certifying and approving payment himself is a segregation conflict (ICA-005).

CAS-053.q: Case – A developer sells apartments with a commitment to 'buy back after 3 years at 110% of price' if buyers wish. Under IFRS 15:
CAS-053.e: When repurchase ≥ selling price and the customer has a significant incentive to exercise, it's a financing.
o: A customer put at a repurchase price above the original price → usually a financing arrangement, no revenue yet
CAS-053.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras B64–B76 (repurchase agreements – customer put options).
Analysis: The customer can require the developer to buy back at 110% > the original price → repurchase price ≥ sale price and above expected market value → significant economic incentive to exercise → accounted for as a financing arrangement (B70, B76): no revenue; cash received is a financial liability and the 10% excess is interest expense.
Distractors: B misstates the substance; C – a 10% provision doesn't reflect financing; D is wrong.

CAS-054.q: Case – Interest on a specific loan for a property project held for sale (long-term inventory) can be capitalised into the project under VAS 16.
CAS-054.e: True. Inventory requiring a substantial period to complete is a qualifying asset.
CAS-054.x:
Basis: VAS 16 paras 06–07 (qualifying assets needing a substantial period); Circular 200/2014/TT-BTC.
Analysis: True. Under VAS 16, borrowing costs directly attributable to constructing or producing assets that take a substantial time (over 12 months) – including property for sale – are capitalised when criteria are met (probable benefits, reliable measurement). For specific loans: actual borrowing costs less temporary investment income on them.
Note: IAS 23 exempts inventories produced repetitively in large quantities.

CAS-055.q: Case – An EPC contractor uses cost-based progress; at year-end it finds total estimated costs were understated from the start due to an obvious calculation error in the budget (information available when last year's FS were prepared). Treatment:
CAS-055.e: Distinguish errors (information available that should have been used) from estimate changes (new information).
o: A prior-period error if material → retrospective restatement; if due to new information → prospective change in estimate
CAS-055.x:
Basis: VAS 29 paras 19–21, 27–29; IAS 8 paras 34–36, 41–43.
Analysis: Distinguish: a prior-period error – failure to use, or misuse of, reliable information available when the prior FS were prepared (an obvious calculation error in the budget) → if material, restate retrospectively with restated comparatives; a change in estimate – from new information or developments → apply prospectively.
Distractors: B – it isn't always an estimate change; C ignores a material error; D is wrong.

CAS-056.q: Case – The auditor finds a builder recognised public-project revenue without acceptance minutes, only 'internal quantity confirmations', to meet profit targets for a bond issue. Select ALL suitable responses:
CAS-056.e: A bond issue creates pressure that raises fraud risk.
o: Assess fraudulent reporting as a significant risk
Require external evidence (employer confirmations, acceptance minutes)
Extend cut-off and period-end journal testing
Communicate incentives and findings with governance
CAS-056.x:
Basis: VSA 240 paras 26–27, 30, 40–42; VSA 505; VSA 260.
Analysis: Public-project revenue booked on 'internal quantity confirmations' only, without acceptance minutes, while profit targets must be hit for a bond issue (pressure) → (A) FS fraud risk is a significant risk; (B) demand external evidence – employer confirmations, acceptance minutes; (C) extend cut-off testing and period-end journal review; (D) communicate the incentive and findings to governance.
Distractors: (E) Internal confirmations aren't independent or sufficient evidence.

CAS-057.q: Case – A developer sells a project by transferring 100% of the project company (price VND 900 billion). The project company's consolidated net assets are 700 billion; transaction costs 10 billion. What is the consolidated gain on disposal (VND billion)?
CAS-057.x:
Basis: IFRS 10 para 25, B97–B99 (loss of control); VAS 25 para 31 (disposal of subsidiaries).
Working: Consolidated gain = proceeds − subsidiary's net assets in the consolidated FS − transaction costs = 900 − 700 − 10 = VND 190 billion.
Analysis: Consolidated FS compare with net assets (including any remaining goodwill – ignored here), not the investment's cost as in separate FS. Selling 100% of a project company may in substance be an asset sale – consider presenting revenue/COGS versus a disposal gain.
Check: 700 + 10 + 190 = 900 ✓.

CAS-058.q: Case – A contractor has a bank-issued performance bond in favour of the employer. In the contractor's FS:
CAS-058.e: Margin deposits are restricted cash requiring disclosure.
o: No liability unless a call is probable; disclose commitments and pledged deposits
Recognise the full bond as a liability
CAS-058.x:
Basis: VAS 18 paras 10–14, 86 (contingent liabilities); IAS 37 paras 27–28, 86.
Analysis: A bank performance guarantee issued to the employer: the contractor records no liability unless the guarantee is likely to be called (breach, delay) – then a provision. Disclose commitments, guarantees and pledged assets; margin deposits are restricted cash (not cash equivalents).
Distractors: B – recording the full guarantee is wrong; C – it isn't revenue; D – disclosure is required.

CAS-059.q: Case – If buyers can cancel apartment contracts and the developer only refunds amounts received without compensation for work done, the developer usually can't recognise revenue over time.
CAS-059.e: True. There's no enforceable right to payment for work completed.
CAS-059.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 para 37, B9–B13 (enforceable right to payment).
Analysis: True. Criterion 35(c) requires an enforceable right to payment for performance to date (including a reasonable margin) if the customer terminates. If on cancellation the developer only keeps or refunds cash received with no compensation for work done → no such right → over-time recognition fails → recognise at handover (CAS-041).

CAS-060.q: Case – A property group has bonds due within 9 months, falling sales cash flows, and is negotiating extensions. The auditor needs to:
CAS-060.e: Plans lacking third-party commitments usually don't remove doubt.
o: Evaluate management's plans (extension, asset sales, fundraising) and their feasibility with evidence; consider material uncertainty over going concern and disclosure
Ignore it since not yet due
CAS-060.x:
Basis: VSA 570 para 16, A16–A18.
Analysis: Bonds maturing in 9 months (within the 12-month horizon) with falling sales cash → events casting doubt. The auditor evaluates management's plans (extension, asset sales, fundraising) and their feasibility with evidence: bondholder agreements, buyer commitments, cash-flow forecasts with tested assumptions. If a material uncertainty remains → consider disclosure and the opinion (AUD-075).
Distractors: B – it falls within 12 months; C is insufficient; D – adverse only if the going-concern basis is inappropriate.
Note: Plans lacking third-party commitments usually can't dispel the doubt.

CAS-061.q: Case – A software firm sells 3-year SaaS prepaid in full, plus a one-off implementation fee (with no distinct benefit apart from using the SaaS). The implementation fee is recognised:
CAS-061.e: Set-up activities transferring no distinct service aren't separate performance obligations.
o: Combined with SaaS, over the contract term (or expected customer life)
CAS-061.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 para 25, B48–B51 (non-refundable upfront fees – set-up activities).
Analysis: A one-off implementation fee where implementation doesn't transfer a distinct service (mere set-up to deliver SaaS) → not a separate performance obligation → an advance for SaaS, recognised over the contract term (or longer if the fee gives a material renewal right).
Distractors: B and C recognise too early; D is wrong.

CAS-062.q: Case – A software firm signs a 3-year SaaS contract of VND 3,600 million plus a 360 million implementation fee (not a distinct service, recognised with the SaaS), starting 01/07. What revenue is recognised in the first year (6 months) (VND million)?
CAS-062.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras 39–41, B48–B51.
Working: Transaction price = 3,600 + 360 = 3,960 million; recognised evenly over 36 months; year 1 (1 Jul–31 Dec) = 3,960 × 6 / 36 = VND 660 million.
Analysis: The remaining 3,300 million is a contract liability (deferred revenue) since cash was collected upfront; the part recognised in the next 12 months (1,320 million) is current.
Check: 660 + 3,300 = 3,960 ✓; 3,960 / 36 = 110 million/month × 6 = 660 ✓.

CAS-063.q: Case – A tech firm capitalises engineers' salaries on a new product. Select ALL criteria to demonstrate for capitalisation (development phase):
o: Intention and ability to complete and use or sell
How the asset will generate future benefits (market)
CAS-063.x:
Basis: VAS 04 para 41; IAS 38 paras 54, 57.
Analysis: Development costs may be capitalised only when all criteria are shown: (A) technical feasibility; (B) intention and ability to complete and use or sell; (C) how future economic benefits arise (a market or internal usefulness); (D) adequate technical and financial resources; (E) reliable cost measurement. Research costs are always expensed.
Distractors: (F) Working hours aren't a recognition criterion (FRD-037).

CAS-064.q: Case – A logistics firm leases 50 trucks for 5 years with no purchase option. Under IFRS 16 (lessee):
CAS-064.e: IFRS 16 removes operating lease classification for lessees (except short-term/low-value exemptions).
o: Recognise a right-of-use asset and lease liability; depreciate the asset, interest on the liability
CAS-064.x:
Basis: IFRS 16 paras 22–26, 29–31, 36–38, 5–8 (exemptions).
Analysis: The lessee recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability (present value of lease payments) at commencement, then depreciates the asset and records interest on the liability. IFRS 16 removes the operating/finance split for lessees except short-term (≤ 12 months) and low-value exemptions. Five-year truck leases don't qualify.
Distractors: B is the IAS 17/VAS 06 operating-lease approach; C and D are wrong.
Note: Under current VAS 06 this may be an operating lease with rent expensed (CAS-032).

CAS-065.q: Case – A freight forwarder sells door-to-door transport, books space with carriers itself, bears the risk of unsold committed space and sets prices. Revenue is recognised:
CAS-065.e: If it merely books space for a commission, revenue is net.
o: Gross (principal) – it controls the service before transfer, bears risk and sets prices
CAS-065.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras B34–B38 (principal versus agent).
Analysis: The forwarder books space itself, bears the risk of unsold committed space ('inventory' risk), sets prices and is primarily responsible to customers → it controls the service before transfer → principal, recognising gross revenue with carrier charges as cost of sales.
Distractors: B applies only to a commission-earning booking agent; C and D are wrong.

CAS-066.q: Case – A 5-star hotel: internal audit reviews room revenue. Select ALL suitable controls/procedures:
CAS-066.e: Unapproved rate changes create revenue fraud opportunities.
o: Daily reconciliation of housekeeping occupancy to the PMS
Reconcile PMS revenue to the GL and receipts (cards, OTAs, cash)
Analyse unusual room 'moves' or 'early departures' by front-desk staff
Let reception change room rates without approval
CAS-066.x:
Basis: COSO 2013 P10, P13; ACFE.
Analysis: Room revenue controls: (A) daily matching of housekeeping occupancy reports to the PMS – catching occupied rooms without revenue (CAS-067); (B) authorised approval of discounts and complimentary rooms; (C) reconciling PMS revenue to the ledger and receipts (cards, OTAs, cash); (D) analysing unusual 'room moves' and 'early departures' by receptionist – concealment tactics.
Distractors: (E) Receptionists editing rates without approval create fraud opportunity.

CAS-067.q: Case – Hotel reconciliation: housekeeping reports 4,380 occupied room-nights in the month, the PMS shows 4,300 revenue room-nights; ADR VND 2 million. How much revenue may be missing (VND million)?
CAS-067.e: (4,380 − 4,300) × 2 = 160 million VND – to be explained (approved comps, recording errors or fraud).
CAS-067.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 P13 (independent operational data matching).
Working: Difference = 4,380 − 4,300 = 80 room-nights; possible missing revenue = 80 × 2 = VND 160 million.
Analysis: Each gap needs explaining: approved complimentary rooms (VIPs, service recovery), recording errors, or fraud – staff letting guests stay for cash not entered in the PMS (skimming – FRD-018).
Check: 4,300 + 80 = 4,380 ✓.

CAS-068.q: Case – A fintech holds customers' e-wallet money in a payment guarantee account. The most important audit risk:
CAS-068.e: Customer fund shortfalls are serious fraud and compliance risks.
o: Reconciling wallet balances to guarantee deposits; risk of using customer funds for operations; IT controls and central bank compliance
CAS-068.x:
Basis: VSA 250; VSA 315; State Bank circulars on payment intermediary services (e-wallet guarantee accounts).
Analysis: Customer e-wallet balances must be 100% backed by the payment guarantee account. Key risk: customer-money shortfalls from use in company operations (fraud, regulatory breach); reconcile total wallet balances to the guarantee deposits; IT controls (wallet data, transactions); State Bank compliance – breaches may lead to licence revocation, affecting going concern.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't fintech-specific risks.

CAS-069.q: Case – A haulier rewards drivers for fuel savings but finds fuel cards used for outside vehicles. Select ALL detective/preventive controls:
o: Link fuel cards to plates, cap litres/day
Match fuel transactions to vehicle GPS location
Analyse usage per vehicle/driver vs standards
Surprise tank checks and unusual transactions (night, off-route)
CAS-069.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 P10, P13 (FRD-021, ICA-091).
Analysis: Fuel card controls: (A) link cards to plates with daily litre caps – preventive; (B) match fuelling transactions to GPS location – a truck not at the station means fuelling another vehicle; (C) analyse consumption by vehicle/driver against standards; (D) surprise tank-capacity checks and review of unusual transactions (night, off-route).
Distractors: (E) Unverified driver self-reporting creates opportunity, especially with a savings bonus (an incentive to under-report).

CAS-070.q: Case – A consulting firm bills by hours; staff enter timesheets and project managers approve. Main risk and control:
CAS-070.e: When bonuses tie to billable hours, pressure to inflate rises.
o: Inflated hours to boost revenue/bonuses; controls: match timesheets to system logs, client confirmation, unusual-hours analytics
CAS-070.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 P5, P10; IFRS 15 (time-based revenue).
Analysis: Revenue recognised from self-entered timesheets with bonuses tied to billable hours → risk of padded hours to boost revenue and bonuses (FS fraud and fraud on clients). Controls: match timesheets with system logs (logins, email, documents), client confirmation of hours, analysis of unusual hours (over 12/day, period-end spikes), independent approval.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the main risk.

CAS-071.q: Case – A tech company granting employee share options (ESOP) under IFRS 2 recognises expense at grant-date fair value over the vesting period.
CAS-071.e: True. The credit goes to equity (equity-settled transaction).
CAS-071.x:
Basis: IFRS 2 paras 10–12, 14–15, 19–20.
Analysis: True. Equity-settled share-based payments (employee options): expense measured at the options' grant-date fair value (not remeasured), spread over the vesting period based on options expected to vest (trued up for service conditions); Dr expense / Cr equity (CAS-072).
Note: VAS has no IFRS 2 equivalent.

CAS-072.q: Case – 100,000 options are granted, grant-date fair value VND 50,000 each, 4-year vesting; 90% of staff expected to vest. What is year-1 expense (VND million)?
CAS-072.x:
Basis: IFRS 2 paras 19–20.
Working: Expected total cost = 100,000 × 90% × 50,000 = VND 4,500,000,000; year-1 expense = 4,500 million / 4 = VND 1,125 million.
Analysis: Later years true up for revised retention: cumulative expense = total × elapsed share − expense already recognised. The VND 50,000 fair value stays fixed (grant date).
Check: 1,125 × 4 = 4,500 ✓.

CAS-073.q: Case – A private hospital: insurer claims are partly rejected after review. Appropriate revenue accounting:
CAS-073.e: Expected rejections reduce the transaction price, distinct from credit risk.
o: Estimate variable consideration (historical rejection rate) at recognition rather than booking all and later providing for bad debts
Recognise all revenue, rejected portion as other expense
Recognise only when the insurer pays
CAS-073.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras 50–54, 56 (variable consideration – implicit price concessions), distinguished from IFRS 9 (credit risk).
Analysis: Health-insurance revenue expected to be rejected after assessment is a price reduction (the hospital accepts less) → estimate it from historical rejection rates at recognition, recognising only what's highly probable not to reverse. This differs from credit risk (inability to pay) – which gets an ECL allowance.
Distractors: B – booking all and expensing rejections inflates revenue; C is too late; D is wrong.

CAS-074.q: Case – An IT services firm outsources its data centre and uses many SaaS tools. The FS auditor should:
CAS-074.e: VSA 402 applies when an entity uses service organisations.
o: Identify service organisations relevant to the FS
Obtain SOC 1/ISAE 3402 reports, assessing coverage and exceptions
Assess data access risks and internal access rights
Skip it as providers are large
CAS-074.x:
Basis: VSA 402 paras 9–16 (AUD-031, ICA-044).
Analysis: An entity using an outsourced data centre and SaaS → the auditor: (A) identifies service organisations affecting the FS (transaction processing, accounting data storage); (B) obtains SOC 1/ISAE 3402 Type 2 reports, assessing coverage periods (gaps – bridge letters) and reported exceptions; (C) tests complementary user entity controls (CUECs); (D) assesses data access risks and internal access rights.
Distractors: (E) A vendor's size doesn't substitute for control evidence.

CAS-075.q: Case – A logistics firm incurs large container repairs in December but the invoices arrive in February. Correct accounting:
CAS-075.e: Accrual basis; this is a test point for unrecorded liabilities.
o: Accrue December cost based on repair acceptance records, without waiting for invoices
CAS-075.x:
Basis: VAS 01 paras 03 (accrual basis), 06 (matching); Circular 200/2014/TT-BTC (accrued expenses).
Analysis: Container repairs performed and accepted in December → a December expense, accrued on the acceptance minutes, contract or quotes (Dr expense / Cr accrued liabilities), without waiting for February's invoice. It is also where auditors look for unrecorded liabilities (AUD-035).
Distractors: B – invoice-based booking uses the wrong period; C omits expense and liability; D – routine repairs don't increase cost (AUD-042).
Note: For CIT, accrued costs must meet valid-document conditions under tax rules.

CAS-076.q: Case – A tech start-up has lost money for 3 years, has 6 months of cash and an uncommitted funding round. The auditor concludes a material uncertainty exists; the FS don't disclose it. The opinion:
CAS-076.e: The 'Material Uncertainty' section applies only when disclosure is adequate.
o: Qualified or adverse (depending on pervasiveness) for inadequate disclosure
CAS-076.x:
Basis: VSA 570 paras 19–20; VSA 705 paras 7–8.
Analysis: A material uncertainty exists (3 years of losses, 6 months of cash, uncommitted new funding) but the FS don't disclose it → a material disclosure misstatement → qualified or adverse depending on pervasiveness. The 'Material uncertainty' paragraph applies only with adequate disclosure (AUD-075).
Distractors: B and C don't fit missing disclosure; D – a disclaimer is for scope limits or rare cases of multiple uncertainties.

CAS-077.q: Case – Restaurant chain: internal audit finds one branch's food cost/revenue at 42% vs a 32% standard. Select ALL lines of enquiry:
CAS-077.e: High food cost may stem from prices, waste, revenue fraud or wrong recipes.
o: Compare purchase prices with central pricing
Check voids, staff meals and unapproved comps
Conclude the chef is committing fraud
CAS-077.x:
Basis: ACFE; COSO 2013 P10, P13.
Analysis: Food cost at 42% versus a 32% standard may stem from: (A) portions exceeding recipes or stock issues not matching recipes; (B) purchase prices above central rates (kickbacks – FRD-024); (C) unapproved voids, staff meals or comps; (D) unrecorded sales (off-POS – skimming) shrinking the denominator.
Distractors: (E) Concluding without evidence (FRD-055).

CAS-078.q: Case – Restaurant chain: one branch has revenue of VND 2,000 million/month and actual food cost of 42% versus a 32% standard. What monthly ingredient cost variance needs explaining (VND million)?
CAS-078.x:
Basis: ACFE (standard variance analysis).
Working: Difference = 2,000 × (42% − 32%) = 2,000 × 10% = VND 200 million/month.
Analysis: That's 2.4 billion a year. Actual food cost 840 million versus an expected 640 million. If the cause is unrecorded sales (CAS-077 D), true sales might be 840 / 32% ≈ 2,625 million → about 625 million/month missing – test both directions.
Check: 2,000 × 42% − 2,000 × 32% = 840 − 640 = 200 ✓.

CAS-079.q: Case – A telco sells a plan with a subsidised phone (VND 0 handset, 24-month commitment at 300 thousand/month). Standalone phone price 4.8 million, standalone plan 300 thousand/month. Revenue on handset delivery under IFRS 15:
o: Allocate the 7.2 million price by standalone prices: phone ≈ 2.88 million upfront (contract asset), the rest over the service period
Zero since the customer pays nothing for the phone
CAS-079.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras 73–80 (relative stand-alone selling price allocation), 107 (contract assets).
Working: Transaction price = 0 + 300k × 24 = 7.2 million; total stand-alone prices = 4.8 + 7.2 = 12 million; phone = 7.2 × 4.8 / 12 = 2.88 million; service = 7.2 × 7.2 / 12 = 4.32 million (≈ 180k/month).
Analysis: On handing over the phone, recognise 2.88 million of revenue (against a contract asset, as no cash is received); service revenue accrues over 24 months; each 300k monthly bill splits into 180k service revenue and 120k reducing the contract asset.
Check: 2.88 + 4.32 = 7.2 ✓; 120 × 24 = 2,880k ✓.

CAS-080.q: Case – Sales commissions paid on winning long-term service contracts (incremental costs of obtaining a contract) may be capitalised and amortised under IFRS 15 if recoverable.
CAS-080.e: True. A practical expedient allows expensing if the amortisation period is ≤ 1 year.
CAS-080.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 paras 91–94 (incremental costs of obtaining a contract), 99 (amortisation).
Analysis: True. Commissions payable only on signing are incremental costs of obtaining a contract → capitalised if expected to be recovered, amortised consistently with service transfer (contract term, possibly including expected renewals) and tested for impairment. Practical expedient: expense immediately if the amortisation period is ≤ 1 year.
Note: Fixed sales salaries incurred regardless of signing aren't capitalised.

CAS-081.q: Case – A 25-subsidiary conglomerate has many intra-group transactions; year-end intra-group reconciliation differences of VND 150 billion are unexplained. Risk and handling:
CAS-081.e: Unexplained intra-group differences often hide errors or fraud.
o: Risk of wrong eliminations and concealed transactions; require transaction-level reconciliation, handle goods in transit, FX differences and one-sided postings before consolidation close
CAS-081.x:
Basis: VAS 25 paras 20–23 (eliminating intragroup items); IFRS 10 para B86; VSA 600.
Analysis: A 150 billion unexplained intragroup reconciliation gap → risks: wrong eliminations (balances not cancelling, gaps 'pushed' elsewhere), concealed transactions, fraud. Action: reconcile transaction by transaction between each pair; identify causes – goods in transit, FX differences, one-sided entries, cut-off; adjust before closing consolidation.
Distractors: B and C – pushing gaps into goodwill or other income is wrong; D – intragroup items can still hide errors.

CAS-082.q: Case – The group auditor uses another auditor for a significant overseas subsidiary. Under VSA 600, the group auditor must:
CAS-082.e: The group auditor is responsible for the consolidated FS opinion.
o: Understand the component auditor's competence and independence, participate in risk assessment, issue instructions, review work papers and results
Only receive the subsidiary's audit report
Bear no responsibility for that work
CAS-082.x:
Basis: VSA 600 paras 11, 19–20, 30–31, 40–42.
Analysis: The group auditor is responsible for the consolidated opinion (no division of responsibility in the report). For component auditors at significant subsidiaries, it must: understand their competence, independence and regulatory environment; be involved in the component risk assessment; issue instructions (component materiality, risks, reporting); review working papers and results and discuss findings.
Distractors: B and C are insufficient and misplace responsibility; D isn't required.
Note: ISA 600 (Revised 2022) stresses a risk-based approach; the current VSA 600 follows the old ISA 600.

CAS-083.q: Case – A group's fund holds 45% of a company but a shareholders' agreement gives it the right to appoint most Board members. Select ALL correct statements:
CAS-083.e: Control is determined by substance (IFRS 10), not just ownership.
o: It may have control despite owning under 50%
Assess power over relevant activities, exposure to variable returns and ability to use power to affect returns
If it controls, it must consolidate
Under 50% ownership is always an associate
CAS-083.x:
Basis: IFRS 10 paras 5–7, B14–B18, B38–B50; VAS 25.
Analysis: Control depends on substance: (B) power over relevant activities, exposure to variable returns and ability to use power to affect them. (A) A 45% stake with shareholder-agreement rights to appoint most board members → control is possible; (C) if controlled → consolidate.
Distractors: (D) Under 50% isn't always an associate – it depends on actual rights.
Note: VAS 25 relies mainly on > 50% voting rights but also recognises control via agreements and board-majority appointment rights.

CAS-084.q: Case – A group buys 60% of a logistics firm for VND 900 billion; net asset fair value 1,200 billion; NCI measured at fair value of 560 billion (IFRS 3, full goodwill). What is goodwill (VND billion)?
CAS-084.e: 900 + 560 − 1,200 = 260 billion VND (the proportionate method would give 900 + 480 − 1,200 = 180).
CAS-084.x:
Basis: IFRS 3 paras 19, 32.
Working: Full goodwill (NCI at fair value): goodwill = consideration 900 + NCI 560 − net assets 1,200 = VND 260 billion. Proportionate method: NCI = 40% × 1,200 = 480 → goodwill = 900 + 480 − 1,200 = 180 billion.
Analysis: The 80 billion difference (560 − 480) is goodwill attributable to NCI. The NCI measurement choice is made per combination.
Note: VAS 11 recognises only the parent's share of goodwill (like the proportionate method) and amortises it over at most 10 years.

CAS-085.q: Case – On an acquisition, the group finds net asset fair value exceeds the price (bargain purchase). Before recognising a gain, IFRS 3 requires:
CAS-085.e: Bargain purchases are rare; they often signal measurement errors.
o: Reassessing identification and measurement of all assets, liabilities, consideration and NCI; any remaining excess goes to profit or loss
CAS-085.x:
Basis: IFRS 3 paras 34–36.
Analysis: A bargain purchase (identifiable net assets > consideration + NCI + previously held interest) is rare and usually signals mismeasurement. Before recognising a gain, the acquirer must reassess identification and measurement of all assets, liabilities (including contingent ones), consideration and NCI. Any remaining excess → gain in profit or loss at acquisition.
Distractors: B – not equity; C – amortisation is an outdated approach, not IFRS 3; D – the reassessment comes first.

CAS-086.q: Case – A group runs cash pooling; cash-rich subsidiaries lend to others via the parent. Select ALL issues to consider:
CAS-086.e: Contracts and proper governance approvals are needed.
o: Eliminate intra-group loans and interest on consolidation
Compliance with lending rules and related-party (tax) rules
Interests of NCI in lending subsidiaries
Credit risk if the borrowing subsidiary struggles (separate FS)
No contracts needed within the group
CAS-086.x:
Basis: VAS 25; Decree 132/2020/ND-CP (related-party transactions, interest deduction cap); IFRS 9; Law on Enterprises 2020 (approval of related-party deals).
Analysis: Cash pooling: (A) eliminate intragroup loans and interest on consolidation; (B) comply with inter-company lending and transfer-pricing rules – market interest rates, the deductible interest cap (30% of EBITDA under Decree 132/2020); (C) protect NCI in the lending subsidiary (cash drained); (D) credit risk on the loan in separate FS if the borrower struggles.
Distractors: (E) Contracts and governance approvals are still required.

CAS-087.q: Case – A group is preparing its first consolidated IFRS FS. The standard governing first-time adoption is:
CAS-087.e: IFRS 1 allows exemptions such as fair value as deemed cost for PP&E.
o: IFRS 1 – First-time Adoption (opening balance sheet, retrospective application with exemptions)
CAS-087.x:
Basis: IFRS 1 paras 2–3, 6–7, 10, 18, appendix D (exemptions).
Analysis: IFRS 1 governs first IFRS financial statements: prepare an opening IFRS balance sheet at the transition date; apply IFRSs effective at the reporting date retrospectively, subject to mandatory exceptions and optional exemptions (e.g., fair value as deemed cost for PP&E, not restating pre-transition business combinations); reconcile equity and profit from VAS to IFRS.
Distractors: B, C and D don't govern first-time adoption.
Note: Vietnam's IFRS roadmap is in Decision 345/QD-BTC (2020); check the updated VFRS plan.

CAS-088.q: Case – Select ALL common differences when converting a Vietnamese group's FS from VAS to IFRS:
CAS-088.e: IFRS still requires consolidating controlled subsidiaries.
o: Leases recognised as ROU assets and lease liabilities (IFRS 16)
Receivable allowances on expected credit losses (IFRS 9)
Financial instruments at fair value in many cases
CAS-088.x:
Basis: IAS 36; IFRS 16; IFRS 9; IFRS 10; VAS 11, VAS 06; Circular 48/2019/TT-BTC.
Analysis: Common VAS → IFRS differences: (A) goodwill – VAS amortises over at most 10 years, IFRS doesn't amortise but tests annually for impairment; (B) leases – VAS 06 has operating leases, IFRS 16 puts right-of-use assets and liabilities on balance sheet; (C) receivable allowances – VAS/Circular 48 by overdue age, IFRS 9 by expected credit loss; (D) financial instruments – IFRS uses fair value in many cases.
Distractors: (E) IFRS 10 still requires consolidating subsidiaries.

CAS-089.q: Case – A conglomerate reports segments under IFRS 8. Segments are identified based on:
o: How information is reported internally to the chief operating decision maker (CODM) to allocate resources and assess performance
CAS-089.x:
Basis: IFRS 8 paras 5, 7, 11–13 (operating segments – management approach); VAS 28.
Analysis: IFRS 8 identifies segments by how information is reported internally to the chief operating decision maker (CODM) to allocate resources and assess performance; quantitative thresholds then apply (10% of revenue, profit/loss or assets; reportable segments ≥ 75% of external revenue).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the basis.
Note: VAS 28 requires business and geographical segments (per the old IAS 14), not a pure management approach.

CAS-090.q: Case – An associate (25% owned) earns VND 400 billion and pays dividends of 120 billion. The opening investment is 1,000 billion. What is the closing equity-method carrying amount (VND billion)?
CAS-090.x:
Basis: VAS 07 para 10; IAS 28 para 10.
Working: Year-end carrying amount = 1,000 + 25% × 400 − 25% × 120 = 1,000 + 100 − 30 = VND 1,070 billion.
Analysis: Under the equity method, the investment rises by the investor's share of profit (100 billion – in consolidated profit) and falls by dividends received (30 billion – not income, a return of investment).
Check: 1,000 + 25% × (400 − 120) = 1,000 + 70 = 1,070 ✓.

CAS-091.q: Case – The group chairman personally owns a security and cleaning company serving the whole group at 20% above market. The Audit Committee should:
CAS-091.e: Governing top-level conflicts is a core Audit Committee duty.
o: Commission an independent related-party review, benchmark prices, check approvals (chairman abstaining) and disclose as required
CAS-091.x:
Basis: Decree 05/2019/ND-CP; Law on Enterprises 2020 Art. 167; VSA 550; COSO 2013 P2.
Analysis: The chair personally owns a vendor serving the whole group at 20% above market → an off-market related-party deal transferring value – a conflict at the very top. The audit committee should commission an independent review (market price comparison, re-tender), check approval under the enterprise law (interested parties abstaining), ensure securities disclosure, and report to the board/AGM.
Distractors: B – group-wide totals may be large and qualitatively material; C is conflicted; D – disclosure doesn't resolve the conflict.

CAS-092.q: Case – A group sets up an Audit Committee under the Board and wants effective internal audit. Select ALL factors ensuring IA independence and effectiveness:
CAS-092.e: CEO control over scope and pay weakens independence.
o: The CAE reports functionally to the Audit Committee, which approves appointment and removal
An internal audit charter approved by the Board, unrestricted access
A risk-based plan with adequate resources
The CEO sets audit scope and the CAE's pay
CAS-092.x:
Basis: IIA GIAS 2024 (Principles 6–8: board authorisation, independent positioning, board oversight); Decree 05/2019/ND-CP Arts. 8–10.
Analysis: Independence and effectiveness factors: (A) the CAE reports functionally to the audit committee, which approves appointment and removal; (B) a board-approved IA charter with unrestricted access; (C) a risk-based, adequately resourced plan; (D) periodic quality assessments – internal and independent external (at least every 5 years per IIA).
Distractors: (E) The CEO setting scope and the CAE's pay weakens independence (ICA-009).
